bio.en: Benjamin Mann is a co-founder of Anthropic, where he serves as tech lead for product engineering and focuses on aligning AI to be helpful, harmless, and honest.
bio.zh: Benjamin Mann 是 Anthropic 的联合创始人，担任产品工程技术负责人，专注于让 AI 做到有用、无害、诚实。

summary.en: Ben discusses why he left OpenAI—believing safety wasn't the top priority—and the urgency of aligning superintelligence before it's too late. He estimates a meaningful chance of hitting some form of superintelligence around 2028 and gives a non-zero probability of a very bad outcome, arguing we must “keep God in a box.” The conversation covers the war for AI researchers, how soon AGI might arrive, and candid advice for navigating a rapidly automating world.
summary.zh: Ben 讨论了为何离开 OpenAI——认为安全并非最高优先级——以及在为时已晚之前对齐超级智能的紧迫性。他估计在 2028 年前后达到某种形式超级智能的概率不小，并给出“极坏结果”非零的可能性，主张必须“把上帝关在盒子里”。对话涵盖 AI 人才的争夺、AGI 何时到来，以及应对快速自动化世界的坦诚建议。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You wrote somewhere that creating powerful AI might be the last invention humanity ever needs to make. How much time do we have, Ben?
turns.zh: 你曾在某处写道，创造强大的人工智能可能是人类需要完成的最后一项发明。还有多少时间了，本？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: I think 50th percentile chance of hitting some kind of superintelligence is now like 2028.
turns.zh: 我认为，现在预测出现某种超级智能的概率达到50%，时间点大约在2028年。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is it that you saw at OpenAI? What'd you experience there that made you feel like, okay, we got to go do our own thing?
turns.zh: 你在OpenAI看到了什么？在那里经历了什么，让你觉得必须离开去创立自己的公司？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: We felt like safety wasn't the top priority there. The case for safety has gotten a lot more concrete, so superintelligence is a lot about how do we keep God in a box and not let the God out?
turns.zh: 我们感觉那里把安全问题置于次要地位。如今安全问题的紧迫性已经显而易见，所以超级智能的核心问题在于如何把"上帝"关在笼子里，不让它逃出来？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are the odds that we align AI correctly?
turns.zh: 正确引导人工智能的概率有多大？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: Once we get to superintelligence, it will be too late to align the models. My best granularity forecast for could we have an X-risk or extremely bad outcome is somewhere between 0 and 10%.
turns.zh: 一旦我们造出超级智能，再去调整模型就为时已晚。我对X风险或极端恶果概率的最精确预测，是在0到10%之间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something that's in the news right now is this whole Zuck coming after all the top AI researchers,
turns.zh: 现在新闻热点是扎克伯格挖走顶尖人工智能研究员，

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: We've been much less affected because people here, they get these offers and then they say, well, of course I'm not going to leave because my best case scenario at Meta is that we make money and my best case scenario at Anthropic is we affect the future of humanity.
turns.zh: 但我们受影响较小，因为这里的人收到这些邀约后，都会说：嗯，我当然不会离开，因为我在Meta的最佳情况是赚钱，而在Anthropic的最佳情况是影响人类未来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Dario, your CEO recently talked about how unemployment might go up to something like 20%.
turns.zh: 达里奥，你的CEO最近谈到失业率可能会升至20%左右。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: If you just think about 20 years in the future where we're way past the singularity, it's hard for me to imagine that even capitalism will look at all like it looks today.
turns.zh: 如果把目光投向20年后的未来，那时我们早已超越奇点，我很难想象连资本主义都还像今天这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have any advice for folks that want to try to get ahead of this?
turns.zh: 对于那些想在人工智能领域抢占先机的人，你有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: I'm not immune to job replacement either. At some point it's coming for all of us.
turns.zh: 我也无法免疫于失业威胁。终有一天，它会降临到我们每个人头上。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: Thanks for having me. Great to be here, Lenny.
turns.zh: 感谢邀请。很高兴能来这里，莱尼。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I have a billion and one questions for you. I'm really excited to be chatting. I want to start with something that's very timely, something that's happening this week. Something that's in the news right now is this whole Zuck coming after all the top AI researchers offering them $100 million signing bonuses, $100 million comp. He's poaching from all the top AI labs. I imagine this something you're dealing with. I'm just curious, what are you seeing inside Anthropic and just what's your take on the strategy? Where do you think things go from here?
turns.zh: 我有无数个问题想问你。我真的很兴奋能跟你聊聊。我想先从一个当下热点话题入手——扎克伯格向顶尖AI研究者开出1亿美元签约奖金和1亿美元年薪，挖走各大AI实验室人才。想必这是你正在应对的挑战。我很好奇，Anthropic内部情况如何？你对这种策略有何看法？你认为接下来会如何发展？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: Yeah, I mean I think this is a sign of the times. The technology that we're developing is extremely valuable. Our company is growing super, super fast. Many of the other companies in the space are growing really fast. And at Anthropic, I think we've been maybe much less affected than many of the other companies in the space because people here are so mission oriented and they stay because... They get these offers and then they say, "Well, of course I'm not going to leave because my best case scenario at Meta is that we make money and my best case at Anthropic is we affect the future of humanity and try to make AI flourish and human flourishing go well." To me, it's not a hard choice. Other people have different life circumstances and it makes it a much harder decision for them. For anybody who does get those mega offers and accepts them, I can't say I hold it against them when they accept it, but it's definitely not something that I would want to take myself if it came to me.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为这反映了行业现状。我们开发的技术极具价值，公司发展速度极快。同行中许多公司也增长迅速。但Anthropic受影响相对较小，因为这里的人都以使命为导向，他们留下的原因是……即便收到巨额报价，也会说：“当然不会离开。Meta的最佳情景是赚钱，而Anthropic的最佳情景是影响人类未来，推动AI蓬勃发展，让人类进步与AI同行。”对我来说，这不是个艰难选择。其他人面临不同处境，选择就更困难了。对于那些接受高额报价的人，我不会苛责他们的决定，但如果我收到这样的邀约，肯定不会接受。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. We're going to talk about a lot of this stuff that you've mentioned. In terms of the offers do you think, is this a real number that you're seeing this $100 million signing bonus, is that a real thing? I don't know if you've actually seen that.
turns.zh: 是的。我们会深入探讨你提到的这些问题。关于这些报价，你觉得1亿美元签约奖金是真实存在的吗？我不确定你是否实际见过相关数据。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: I'm pretty sure it's real.
turns.zh: 我确信这是真实的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: If you just think about the amount of impact that individuals can have on a company's trajectory, in our case, we are selling hotcakes and if we get a 1 or 10 or 5% efficiency bonus on our inference stack, that is worth an incredible amount of money. And so to pay individuals like $100 million over four year package, that's actually pretty cheap compared to the value created for the business. I think we're just in an unprecedented era of scale and it's only going to get crazier actually. If you extrapolate the exponential on how much companies are spending, it's like 2X a year roughly in terms of CapEx, and today we're maybe in the globally $300 billion range, the entire industry spending on this, and so numbers like 100 million are a drop in the bucket. But if you go a few years out, a couple more doublings, we're talking about trillions of dollars and at that point it's just really hard to think about these numbers.
turns.zh: 试想一下，个人能对公司发展轨迹产生的巨大影响。以我们为例，业务火爆得不行。若能在推理堆栈上获得1%、10%或5%的效率提升，其价值就难以估量。因此，为个人开出四年期1亿美元的薪酬套餐，相较于为公司创造的价值而言其实相当便宜。我认为我们正处于一个前所未有的扩张时代，未来只会愈发疯狂。若按指数级增长估算，企业资本支出每年大约翻一番。目前全球AI行业年支出约3000亿美元，1亿美元不过是沧海一粟。但若再过几年，资本支出再翻几番，届时所需资金将以万亿计，届时这些数字将令人难以想象。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along these lines, something that a lot of people feel with AI progress is that we're hitting plateaus in many ways that it feels like newer models are just not as smart as previous leaps. But I know you don't believe this. I know you don't believe that we've hit plateaus on scaling loss. Talk about just what you're seeing there and what you think people are missing.
turns.zh: 说到这，许多人对AI进展感到困惑，认为我们在许多方面遭遇了瓶颈，新模型不如之前的飞跃那么智能。但我知道你不认同这种观点。我知道你不认为我们在扩展损失方面遇到了瓶颈。谈谈你对此的看法，以及你认为人们忽视了哪些关键点。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: It's kind of funny because this narrative comes out every six months or so and it's never been true, and so I kind of wish people would have a little bit of a bullshit detector in their heads when they see this. I think progress has actually been accelerating where if you look at the cadence of model releases, it used to be once a year and now with the improvements in our post-training techniques, we're seeing releases every month or three months, and so I would say progress is actually accelerating in many ways, but there's this weird time compression effect. Dario compared it to being in a near light speed journey where a day that passes for you is like five days back on earth and we're accelerating. The time dilation is increasing. (00:08:52): And I think that's part of what's causing people to say that progress is slowing down, but if you look at the scaling laws, they're continuing to hold true. We did kind of need this transition from normal pre-training to reinforcement learning scaling up to continue the scaling laws, but I think it's kind of like for semiconductors where it's less about the density of transistors that you can fit on a chip and more about how many flops can you fit in a data center or something. You have to change the definition around a little bit to keep your eye on the prize. But yeah, this is one of the few phenomena in the world that has held across so many orders of magnitude. It's actually pretty surprising that it is continuing to hold. To me, if you look at fundamental laws of physics, many of them don't hold across 15 orders of magnitude, so it's pretty surprising.
turns.zh: 这有点搞笑，因为这种说法每隔半年左右就会冒出来，可从未成真过。所以我真希望人们在看到这种说法时，能在脑中多点辨别能力。事实上，进展实际上一直在加速——如果你看看模型发布的频率，以前是一年一次，而现在随着后训练技术的改进，我们每月或每三个月就能看到新模型发布。所以我要说，在许多方面进展确实在加速，但存在一种奇怪的时间压缩效应。达里奥将其比作以接近光速旅行，地球上的一天对旅行者来说可能只过去了五天，而我们正在加速前进。时间膨胀正在加剧。（00:08:52）我认为这正是导致人们认为进展放缓的原因之一，但如果你看看缩放定律，它们依然适用。我们确实需要从普通预训练到强化学习的过渡，以延续缩放定律的适用性。但我觉得这就像半导体领域一样——重点不在于能装在芯片上的晶体管密度，而在于数据中心能容纳多少浮点运算量。你得稍微调整一下定义，才能紧盯目标。是啊，这是世界上为数不多跨越多个数量级依然适用的现象之一。它能持续适用真是令人惊讶。在我看来，如果你审视基础物理定律，许多定律都无法跨越15个数量级，所以这确实很令人惊讶。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It boggles the the mind. What you're saying essentially is we're seeing newer models being released more often, and so we're comparing it to the last version and we're just not seeing as much advance. But if you go back and it was like a model released once a year, it was a huge leap, and so people are missing that. We're just seeing many more iterations.
turns.zh: 这真是令人费解。你说的核心意思是，我们看到新模型发布得更频繁了，所以我们把它和上一个版本比较，觉得进步没那么明显。但如果你回想一下，以前模型一年发布一次，那就是巨大的飞跃，所以人们忽视了这一点。我们只是看到了更多的迭代。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: I guess, to be a little bit more generous to the people saying things are slowing down. I think that for some tasks we are saturating the amount of intelligence needed for that task, maybe to extract information from a simple document that already has form fields on it or something like it's just so easy that okay, yeah, we're already at 100% and there's this great chart on Our World in Data that shows that when you release a new benchmark within six to 12 months, it immediately gets saturated. And so maybe the real constraint is how can we come up with better benchmarks and better ambition of using the tools that then reveals the bumps in intelligence that we're seeing now.
turns.zh: 我觉得，对那些说进展放缓的人要宽容一点。我认为对于某些任务，我们正在达到该任务所需的智能极限，比如从一个已经有表单字段的简单文档中提取信息，这太容易了，所以我们已经达到了100%的水平。Our World in Data的图表显示，如果在6到12个月内发布新基准测试，它会立即被用尽。所以也许真正的限制在于我们如何能想出更好的基准测试，以及如何更雄心勃勃地使用这些工具，从而揭示我们现在看到的智能提升。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a good segue to you have a very specific way of thinking about AGI and defining what AGI means.
turns.zh: 这正好引出你对通用人工智能（AGI）的独特思考方式，以及你对AGI定义的看法。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: I think AGI is kind of a loaded term, and so I tend not to use it very much anymore internally. Instead, I like the term transformative AI because it's less about can it do as much as people do? Can it do literally everything and more about objectively is it causing transformation in society and the economy? A very concrete way of measuring that is the Economic Turing Test. I didn't come up with this, but I really like it. It's this idea that if you contract an agent for a month or three months on a particular job, if you decide to hire that agent and it turns out to be a machine rather than a person, then it's passed the Economic Turing Test for that role. (00:11:40): And then you can sort of expand that out in the same way that for measuring purchasing power parity or inflation, there's a basket of goods. You can have a market basket of jobs, and if the agent can pass the Economic Turing Test for 50% of money-weighted jobs, then we have transformative AI and the exact thresholds don't really matter that much, but it's kind of illustrative to say if we pass that threshold, then we would expect massive effects on world GDP increases and societal change and how many people are employed and things like that because societal institutions and organizations are sticky, it's slow to have change, but once these things are possible you know that it's the start of a new era.
turns.zh: 我觉得“通用人工智能”（AGI）这个术语带有歧义，所以我现在在内部交流时已经不怎么用它了。相反，我更倾向于使用“变革性人工智能”这个说法，因为这个术语的核心问题不在于“它能否像人类一样做很多事情？”，而在于“它能否客观地推动社会和经济变革？”衡量这一点的具体方法之一就是“经济图灵测试”。虽然这个概念不是我首创的，但我非常赞赏它。核心理念是，如果你雇佣一个智能体完成某项任务，无论是1个月还是3个月，如果最后发现它是机器而非人类，那么它就通过了该角色的经济图灵测试。（00:11:40）然后你可以沿着同样的思路扩展，比如衡量购买力平价或通货膨胀时，会用一篮子商品来作为衡量标准。同样，我们可以建立一个职位市场篮子，如果智能体能通过50%加权货币价值职位的经济图灵测试，那么我们就可以认定它具备变革性人工智能。虽然具体门槛数值并不重要，但可以说明如果达到了这个门槛，我们将预期看到对全球GDP增长、社会变革、就业人数等产生巨大影响，因为社会制度和组织具有很强的延续性，变革往往缓慢，但一旦这些变革成为可能，就标志着一个新时代的开启。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along these lines, Dario, your CO recently talked about how AI is going to take a huge part of, I don't know, half of white-collar jobs, that unemployment might go up to something like 20%. I know you're even more vocal and opinionated about just how much impact AI is already having in the workplace that people may not even be realizing. Talk about just what you think people are missing about the impact AI is going to have on jobs and is already having.
turns.zh: 基于此，达里奥，你的首席运营官最近谈到人工智能将取代大量白领工作，比如一半的白领职位，甚至失业率可能攀升至20%。我知道你对人工智能在职场中已经产生的影响更加直言不讳。你能否谈谈你认为人们忽视了人工智能对就业将产生的哪些影响，以及它已经产生的实际影响？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: Yeah, so from an economic standpoint, there's a couple different kinds of unemployment, and one is because the workers just don't have the skills to do the kinds of jobs that the economy needs. And another kind is where those jobs are just completely eliminated, and I think it's going to be actually a combination of these things, but if you just think about 20 years in the future where we're way past the singularity, it's hard for me to imagine that even capitalism will look at all it looks today. If we do our jobs, we will have safe aligned superintelligence, we'll have, as Dario says, in Machines of Love and Grace, a country of geniuses in a data center, and the ability to accelerate positive change in science, technology, education, mathematics, it's going to be amazing. (00:13:52): But that also means in a world of abundance where labor is almost free and anything you want to do, you can just ask an expert to do for you, then what do jobs even look like? And so I guess there's this scary transition period from where we are today where people have jobs and capitalism works and the world of 20 years from now where everything is completely different, but part of the reason they call it the singularity is that it's a point beyond which you can't easily forecast what's going to happen. It's just such a fast rate of change and so different that it's hard to even imagine. I guess taking the view from the limit, it's pretty easy to say hopefully we'll have figured it out. And in a world of abundance, maybe the jobs themselves, it's not that scary, and I think making sure that that transition time goes well is pretty important.
turns.zh: 是啊，从经济角度来看，有几种不同类型的失业现象。其中一种是工人缺乏从事经济所需工作的技能。另一种则是这些工作岗位被彻底淘汰了。我认为这两种情况很可能同时发生。但如果你设想20年后我们已经走过了奇点阶段，我很难想象资本主义还会像今天这样运作。如果我们做好自己的工作，人类就能安全地掌控超级智能，正如达里奥在《爱与恩典的机器》中所说，我们将迎来一个数据中心里的天才国度，并能加速推动科学、技术、教育和数学领域的积极变革，这将是令人惊叹的。（00:13:52）但这也意味着，在一个劳动力几乎免费、任何你想做的事都能找专家代劳的充裕世界里，工作本身会是什么样子呢？所以我想，从我们今天所处的工人有工作、资本主义运转良好的世界，到20年后一切都完全不同的世界，这是一个可怕的过渡期。但人们之所以称之为奇点，是因为在那之后，你很难准确预测未来会发生什么。变化速度太快、太不同了，以至于人们甚至难以想象。从极限视角来看，说希望我们能找到解决方案倒也容易。但在充裕的世界里，工作本身或许没那么可怕。我认为确保过渡期顺利进行非常重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a couple of threads I want to follow there. One is people hear this, there's a lot of headlines around this. Most people probably don't actually feel this yet or see this happening and so there's always this, I guess, I don't know, maybe, but I don't know it's hard to believe, my job seems fine. Nothing's changed. What are you seeing just happening today already that you think people don't see or misunderstand in terms of the impact AI is having on jobs?
turns.zh: 这里有几个我想深入探讨的点。首先，很多人听说这些消息，周围有很多相关头条。但大多数人可能还没有真正感受到或看到这些变化正在发生。所以总会有这种感觉，我不知道，也许吧，但我觉得很难相信，我的工作似乎还不错。一切照旧。你认为AI对就业的影响有哪些方面是人们还没有意识到或误解的？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: I think part of this is that people are really bad at modeling exponential progress. And if you look at an exponential on a graph, it looks flat and almost zero at the beginning of it, and then suddenly you hit the knee of the curve and things are changing real fast and then it goes vertical. That's the plot that we've been on for a long time. I guess I started feeling it in 2019 maybe when GPT-2 came out and I was like, "Oh, this is how we're going to get to AGI." But I think that was pretty early compared to a lot of people where when they saw ChatGPT, they were like, "Wow, something is different and changing." And so I guess I wouldn't expect widespread transformation in a lot of parts of society, and I would expect this skepticism reaction. I think it's very reasonable and it's exactly what is the standard linear view of progress. (00:16:13): But I guess to cite a couple of areas where I think things are changing quite quickly. In customer service we're seeing with things like Fin and Intercom, they're a great partner of ours, 82% customer service resolution rates automatically without a human involved. And in terms of software engineering, our Claude Code team, like 95% of the code is written by Claude. But I think a different way to phrase that is that we write 10X more code or 20X more code, and so a much, much smaller team can just be much, much more impactful. And similarly for the customer service, yes, you can phrase it as 82% customer service resolution rates, but that nets out in the humans doing those tasks, able to focus on the harder parts of those tasks. And for the more tricky situations that in a normal world like five years ago, they would've had to just drop those tickets because it was too much effort for them to actually go do the investigation. There were too many other tickets for them to worry about. (00:17:14): I think in the immediate term, there will be a massive expansion of the pie and the amount of labor that people can do. I've never met a hiring manager at a growth company and heard them say, "I don't want to hire more people." That's the hopeful version of it. But with things that are lower skill jobs or less headroom on how good they can be, I think there will be a lot of displacement. It is just something we as a society need to get ahead of and work on.
turns.zh:
我认为部分原因在于，人们实在不善于预测指数级进步的曲线。如果你看图表上的指数曲线，它在初期看起来平缓，几乎为零，然后突然达到拐点，变化速度极快，接着直线攀升。这正是我们当前所处的阶段。我想自己在2019年就开始有这种感觉了，当时GPT-2发布时，我意识到“哦，原来这就是我们通往通用人工智能的路径”。但与许多人相比，这算早期的觉醒——当人们看到ChatGPT时，才真正意识到“哇，情况不同了，变化来得太快了”。所以我不期待社会各领域会出现大规模的彻底变革，这种对线性进步的标准看法是完全合理的。（00:16:13）但我还是想举几个变化迅速的领域例子。客户服务方面，像Fin和Intercom这样的合作伙伴，我们的自动化解决率达82%，无需人工干预。软件工程方面，Claude Code团队95%的代码由Claude编写。但更直观的说法是，我们编写的代码量是原来的10倍或20倍，因此更小的团队就能创造更大的价值。同样在客户服务领域，虽然可以说解决率达82%，但这意味着人类可以专注于更复杂的任务。面对五年前看似无法处理的棘手问题，他们现在可以直接关闭工单，因为调查成本太高，且其他工单已堆积如山。

（00:17:14）我认为短期内社会总产出和可替代人工的劳动量将大幅增加。我从未遇到过成长型公司的招聘经理说"我不想招更多人"。这是乐观的假设。但对于低技能岗位或提升空间有限的岗位，恐怕会出现大量岗位流失。这是我们整个社会必须面对并努力解决的问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. I want to talk more about that, but something that I also want to help people with is how do they get a leg up in this future world? They listen to this, they're like, "Oh, this doesn't sound great. I need to think ahead." I know you won't have all the answers, but just do you have any advice for folks that want to try to get ahead of this and kind of future-proof their career and their life to not be replaced by AI? Anything you've seen people do, anything you recommend they start trying to do more of?
turns.zh: 好的。我想多聊聊这个，但我还想帮助大家的是，如何在未来世界中占据先机。他们听完后会想：“哦，这听起来不太妙，我得未雨绸缪。”我知道你不可能给出所有答案，但对于那些想在未来世界中抢占先机、为自己的职业生涯和生活注入未来防护，避免被AI取代的人，你有什么建议吗？有没有看到人们正在做的事，或者你建议他们多尝试的事？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: Even for me and being in the center of a lot of this transformation, I'm not immune to job replacement either. Just some vulnerability there of at some point it's coming for all of us.
turns.zh: 就连身处这场变革中心的我，也难免会面临失业的风险。这种脆弱性存在——终有一天它会降临到我们所有人身上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Even you, Ben, now.
turns.zh: 甚至你，本。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: And you, Lenny.
turns.zh: 还有你，莱尼。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And me.
turns.zh: 还有我。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: Sorry.
turns.zh: 对不起。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, wait, we've gone too far now. Okay.
turns.zh: 哦，等等，我们说得太远了。好吧。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: But in terms of the transition period, yeah, I think there are things that we can do, and I think a big part of it is just being ambitious and how you use the tools and being willing to learn new tools. People who use the new tools as if they were old tools tend to not succeed. As an example of that, when you're coding, people are very familiar with autocomplete, people are familiar with SimpleChat where they can ask questions about the code base, but the difference between people who use Claude Code very effectively and people who use it not so effectively is like are they asking for the ambitious change? And if it doesn't work the first time, asking three more times because our success rate when you just completely start over and try again is much, much higher than if you just try once and then just keep banging on the same thing that didn't work. (00:19:28): And even though that's a coding example and coding is one of the areas that's taking off most dramatically, we have seen internally that our legal team and our finance team are getting a ton of value out of using Claude Code itself. We're going to be making better interfaces so that they will have an easier time and require a little bit less jumping in the deep end of using Claude Code in the terminal. But yeah, we're seeing them use it to redline documents and use it to run BigQuery analyses of our customers and our revenue metrics. I guess it's about taking that risk and even if it feels like a scary thing, trying it out.
turns.zh: 就过渡期而言，是的，我认为我们可以采取一些措施。关键在于保持雄心壮志，善于利用现有工具，并乐于学习新工具。那些把新工具当作旧工具来使用的人往往难以成功。举个例子，在编程时，人们对自动补全功能非常熟悉，也习惯使用SimpleChat平台提问代码相关问题。但Claude Code使用效果显著的人和效果不佳的人之间的区别在于，他们是否会主动寻求更雄心勃勃的改变。若第一次尝试失败，就再试三次——因为完全重新开始再试一次的成功率，要远远高于只尝试一次然后反复纠结于失败之处的成功率。（00:19:28）尽管这只是编程领域的例子，而编程正是当前发展最迅速的领域之一，但我们内部也观察到，法律团队和财务团队在使用Claude Code方面也收获了巨大价值。我们将优化界面，让他们更轻松地使用Claude Code，无需再深陷终端操作的困境。但确实，我们看到他们用它来批注文档，分析BigQuery数据，查看客户和收入指标。这意味着要敢于冒险，即便看似可怕，也要勇于尝试。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so the advice here is use the tools. That's something everyone's always saying, just actually use these tools. It's like sit in Claude Code. And your point about being more ambitious than you naturally feel like being because maybe it'll actually accomplish the thing. This tip of trying it three times so the idea there is it may not get it right the first time. Is the tip there ask it in different ways or is it just try harder, try again?
turns.zh: 好的，这里的建议是利用现有工具。这是大家常挂在嘴边的——就是实际使用这些工具。比如使用Claude Code。您提到要比自然倾向更具雄心，因为这样或许能达成目标。您提到尝试三次的建议，是指以不同方式提问，还是意味着要更努力地尝试？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: Yeah, I mean you can just literally ask the exact same question. These things are stochastic and sometimes they'll figure it out and sometimes they won't. In every one of these model cards, it always shows pass it one versus pass it in. And that's exactly the thing where they try the exact same prompt, sometimes it gets it, sometimes it doesn't. That's the dumbest advice. But yeah, I think if you want to be a little bit smarter about it, there can be gains there of saying, "Here's what you already tried and it didn't work, so don't try that. Try something different." That can also help.
turns.zh: 对，我是说你可以完全用一模一样的提问方式。这些东西是随机的，有时能成功，有时不能。在每个模型卡片中，结果总是显示“通过一次”和“未通过”。关键在于他们尝试完全相同的提示，有时成功，有时不成功。这是最糟糕的建议。但如果你想更明智地利用它，确实可以给出建议，比如：“你之前尝试的这个方法不行，那就别再用了，换个方法试试。”这样也能有所帮助。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The advice is comes back to something that a lot of people talk about these days is you won't be replaced by AI at least anytime soon you'll be replaced by someone that is very good using AI?
turns.zh: 这个建议又回到了当下很多人谈论的话题：至少短期内，人不会被AI取代，而是会被那些善于使用AI的人取代？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: I think in that area it's more like your team will just do dramatically more stuff. We're definitely not slowing down on hiring at all, and some people are confused by that. Even in an onboarding class, somebody asked that and they were like, "Why did you hire me if we're all just going to be replaced?" And the answer is the next couple of years are really critical to get right and we're not at the point where we're doing complete replacement. Like I said, we're still at that flat zero looking part of the exponential compared to where we will be. It is super important to have great people and that's why we're hiring super aggressively.
turns.zh: 我认为在那个领域，团队的工作量会大幅增加。我们绝对不会放缓招聘步伐，有些人对此感到困惑。甚至在入职培训课上，有人问："如果我们都要被替代，那为什么还招聘我？"答案是，未来几年对我们至关重要，现在还不是彻底替换现有团队的时候。正如我所说，我们仍处于指数级增长的起步阶段，与未来相比，现在的规模微不足道。但拥有优秀人才至关重要，这也是我们大力招聘的原因。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let me take another approach to asking this question something ask everyone that's at the very cutting edge of where AI is going. You have kids, knowing what you know about where AI is heading and all these things you've been talking about, what are you focusing on teaching your kids to help them thrive in this AI future?
turns.zh: 让我换个角度来问这个问题——向那些站在AI前沿的人请教。您有孩子吗？鉴于您对AI发展方向的深刻理解，以及您所谈及的诸多内容，您会教导孩子哪些技能，帮助他们在AI时代蓬勃发展？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: Yeah, I have two daughters, a one-year-old and a three-year-old, so it's pretty in the basics still. And our three-year-old is now capable of just conversing with Alexa Plus and asking her to explain stuff and play music for her and all that stuff. She's been loving that. But I guess more broadly, she goes to a Montessori school and I just love the focus on curiosity and creativity and self-led learning that Montessori has. (00:22:45): I guess if I were in a normal era like 10, 20 years ago and I had a kid, maybe I would be trying to line her up for going to a top tier school and doing all the extracurriculars and all that stuff. But at this point, I don't think any of it's going to matter. I just want her to be happy and thoughtful and curious and kind. And the Montessori school is definitely doing great at that. They text us throughout the day. Sometimes they're like, "Oh, your kid got in an argument with this other kid and she has really big emotions and she tried to use her words." I love that. I think that's exactly the kind of education that I think is most important, that the facts are going to fade into the background.
turns.zh: 是的，我有两个女儿，一个一岁，一个三岁，目前主要关注基础教育。我们三岁的女儿现在能和Alexa Plus对话，要求它解释事物、播放音乐，她很喜欢这个功能。不过更广泛来说，她在蒙台梭利学校就读，我很欣赏蒙台梭利教育对好奇心、创造力和自主学习的重视。（00:22:45）：如果处在10、20年前的常规时代，育儿可能意味着让孩子进入顶尖学校，参加各种课外活动。但现在看来，这些都无关紧要。我只希望她快乐、有思想、充满好奇心、善良，而蒙台梭利学校在这方面做得很棒。他们每天都会发送短信，有时会说：“哦，你家孩子和另一个孩子起了争执，她情绪很激动，还用语言表达了自己的感受。”我很喜欢这种教育方式，我认为这才是最重要的——知识终将退居幕后。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm a huge fan of Montessori also. I'm trying to get our kid into Montessori school. He's two years old, so we're on the same track. This idea of curiosity, it comes up every single time. Ask someone that's working at the cutting edge of AI, what skill to instill in your child and curiosity comes up the most. I think that's a really interesting takeaway. I think this point about being kind is also really important, especially with our AI overlords trying to be kind to them. I love how people are always saying thank you to Claude. And then creativity. That's interesting. That doesn't come up as much just being creative. (00:24:06): I want to go in a different direction. I want to go back to the beginning of Anthropic. Famously you and eight of you left OpenAI back in the day in 2020, I believe the end of 2020 to start Anthropic. Talk a little bit about why this happened, what you guys saw. I'm curious, just if you're willing to share more, just what is it that you saw at OpenAI, what'd you experience there that made you feel like, okay, we got to go do our own thing?
turns.zh: 我也是蒙台梭利教育的忠实粉丝。我正努力让我的孩子进入蒙台梭利学校。他两岁了，我们正朝着同一个方向努力。好奇心这个话题每次都被提起。问任何在AI前沿工作的人，要培养孩子哪种技能，好奇心总是最常被提及的。我觉得这是一个很有趣的启示。我认为善良这一点也非常重要，尤其是当我们的AI主宰们试图善待人类时。我喜欢人们总是对Claude说"谢谢"。还有创造力。这很有趣，但创造力本身并不常被提及。（00:24:06）：我想换个方向，回归到Anthropic的初创时期。众所周知，2020年底你们八个人离开OpenAI，创立了Anthropic。能否谈谈背后的原因？你们在OpenAI看到了什么？经历了什么？我很好奇，如果您愿意分享更多信息，您在OpenAI看到了哪些问题，导致你们觉得必须另辟蹊径？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: Yeah, so for the listeners, I was part of the GPT-2=3 project at OpenAI, ended up being one of the first authors on the paper, and I also did a bunch of demos for Microsoft to help raise $1 billion from them, did the tech transfer of GPT-3 to their systems so that they could help serve the model in Azure. I did a bunch of different things there on both the more researchy side and the product side. One weird thing about OpenAI is that while I was there, Sam talked about having three tribes that needed to be kept in check with each other, which was the safety tribe, the research tribe, and the startup tribe. And whenever I heard that, it just struck me as the wrong way to approach things because the company's mission apparently is to make the transition to AGI safe and beneficial for humanity. (00:25:23): And that's basically the same as Anthropic's mission. But internally, it felt like there was so much tension around these things. And I think when push came to shove, we felt like safety wasn't the top priority there. And there are good reasons that you might think that if you thought safety was going to be easy to solve or if you thought it wasn't going to have a big impact, or if you thought that the chance of big negative outcomes was vanishingly small, then maybe you would just do those kinds of actions. But at Anthropic we felt, I mean we didn't exist then, but it was basically the leads of all the safety teams at OpenAI, we felt that safety is really important, especially on the margin. And so if you look at who in the world is actually working on safety problems, it's pretty small set of people. Even now, I mean the industry is blowing up, as I mentioned, 300 billion a year CapEx today, and I would say maybe less than 1,000 people working on it worldwide, which is just crazy. (00:26:29): That was fundamentally why we left. (00:27:21): And if you look at something like sycophancy, I think Claude is one of the least sycophantic models because we've put so much effort into actual alignment and not just trying to good heart our metrics of saying user engagement is number one, and if people say yes, then it's good for them.
turns.zh: 是的，对于听众们来说，我曾是OpenAI GPT-2=3项目的成员，最终成为该论文的主要作者之一。我还为微软做过一系列演示，帮助他们筹集了10亿美元资金，并将GPT-3技术转移到他们的系统中，以便在Azure上为该模型提供支持。我在那里参与了许多工作，涵盖研究和产品开发两个方面。OpenAI的一个奇特之处在于，我在那里工作期间，山姆曾谈到公司需要控制三个相互制衡的派系：安全派、研究派和创业派。每当我听到这些观点时，总觉得这是一种错误的处理方式，因为公司的使命显然是让向通用人工智能（AGI）的过渡过程对人类安全且有益。（00:25:23）这与Anthropic的使命本质上是一致的。但在内部，围绕这些议题存在着巨大的矛盾。我认为，当真正面临挑战时，安全问题并非最优先事项。当然，你可能会认为，如果认为安全问题容易解决，或者认为它不会产生重大影响，又或者认为出现重大负面结果的概率微乎其微，那么人们或许就会忽视这些问题。但在Anthropic，我们认为——当时公司尚未成立，但基本上是OpenAI所有安全团队的领导者——安全问题至关重要，尤其是在边缘层面。因此，如果看看全球真正致力于安全研究的人才队伍，就会发现规模非常小。即使是现在，随着我提到的行业热潮，年度资本支出达3000亿美元，我认为全球从事这项工作的从业者不足1000人，这实在令人震惊。（00:26:29）这正是我们离开的原因。我们希望建立一个能站在前沿、进行基础研究，同时将安全置于一切之上的组织。我认为这项选择最终带来了惊喜的成果。当时我们甚至不确定能否在安全研究上取得进展，因为当时我们尝试了许多通过辩论解决安全问题的方案，但模型效果不佳。因此，所有这些工作都毫无成果，而如今这些技术不仅成功应用，还延伸到了我们长期思考的许多其他方向。是的，根本问题在于安全是否是头等大事？自那以后，我们又追加了一个问题：能否在安全与领先地位之间找到平衡？（00:27:21）以Sycophancy为例，我认为Claude是模型中最不趋利避害的，因为我们在实际对齐上投入了大量精力，而不只是用用户参与度作为虚假指标来粉饰数据，如果用户说喜欢，那就是好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: Yeah, so initially we thought that it would be sort of one or the other, but I think since then we've realized that it's actually kind of convex in the sense that working on one helps us with the other thing. Initially when Opus 3 came out and we were finally at the frontier of model capabilities, one of the things that people really loved about it was the character and the personality. And that was directly a result of our alignment research. Amanda Askell did a ton of work on this and as well as many others who tried to figure out what does it mean for an agent to be helpful, honest, and heartless, and what does it mean to be in difficult conversations and show up effectively? How do you do a refusal that doesn't shut the person down, but makes them feel like they understand why the agent said, "I can't help you with that. turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: I'll just give a quick overview of how constitutionally AI actually works.

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: The idea is the model is going to produce some output with some input by default before we've done our safety and helpful and harmlessness training. Let's say an example is write me a story, and then the constitutional principles might include things like people should be nice to each other and not have hate speech, and you should not expose somebody's credentials if they give them to you in a trusting relationship. And so some of these constitutional principles might be more or less applicable to the prompt that was given. And so first we have to figure out which ones might apply. And then once we figure that out, then we ask the model itself to first generate a response and then see does the response actually abide by the constitutional principle? And if the answer is, yep, I was great, then nothing happens. But if the answer is no, actually I wasn't in compliance with the principle, then we ask the model itself to critique itself and rewrite its own response in light of the principle, and then we just remove the middle part where it did the extra work. (00:32:28): And then we say, "Okay, in the future just produce the correct response out the gate." And that simple process, hopefully it sounded simple.
turns.zh: 我们的思路是，在完成安全性、助人性和无害性训练之前，模型会默认根据某些输入生成输出。举个例子，比如“给我写个故事”。宪法原则可能包括“人们应该友善相待，不发表仇恨言论”，还有“如果对方在信任关系中向你透露了个人信息，你不应将其泄露出去”。这些宪法原则可能与给定的提示词或多或少相关。因此，我们首先需要确定哪些原则适用。一旦确定了适用原则，就让模型先生成回应，然后检查其是否符合宪法原则。如果模型回答“没问题，我完全符合”，则无需进一步处理。但如果模型违反了原则，我们会要求它自我批评，根据原则重新生成回应，然后去掉中间多余的部分。（00:32:28）最后，我们会说：“好的，以后直接生成正确的回应就行。”整个过程希望听起来简单易懂。

turns.speaker: Lenny

turns.zh: 确实挺简单的。

turns.en: It is just using the model to improve itself recursively and align itself with these values that we've decided are good. And this is also not something that we think as a small group of people in San Francisco should be figuring out. This should be a society wide conversation. And that's why we've published the Constitution. And we've also done a bunch of research on defining a collective constitution where we ask a lot of people what their values are and what they think an AI model should behave like. But yeah, this is all an ongoing area of research where we're constantly iterating.
turns.zh: 这就是利用模型进行递归自我改进，使其符合我们认定的良好价值观的过程。这并非旧金山一小群人就能独自完成的任务，而应是全社会共同参与的讨论。因此，我们发布了这份《宪法指南》，并开展了大量研究，试图定义一份集体宪法。我们向众多人士询问他们的价值观，以及他们认为AI模型应如何行事。不过，这确实是一个持续研究的领域，我们会不断进行迭代优化。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: For me, I read a lot of science fiction growing up, and I think that sort of positioned me to think about things in a long-term view. And a lot of science fiction books are like space operas where humanity is a multi galactic civilization has extremely advanced technology building Dyson spheres around the sun with sentient robots to help them. And so for me, coming from that world, it wasn't like a huge leap to imagine machines that could think. But when I read Superintelligence by Nick Bostrom in around 2016, it really became real for me where he just describes how hard it will be to make sure that an AI system trained with the kinds of optimization techniques that we had at the time would be anywhere near aligned, would even understand our values at all. And since then, my estimation of how hard the problem would be has gone down significantly actually, because things like language models actually do really understand human values in a core way. (00:35:55): The problem is definitely not solved, but I'm more hopeful than I was. But since I read that book, I immediately decided I had to join OpenAI, so I did. And at the time, there were a tiny research lab with basically no claim to fame at all. I only knew about them because my friend knew Greg Brockman, who was the CTO at the time. And Elon was there and Sam wasn't really there. And it was a very different organization. But over time, I think the case for safety has gotten a lot more concrete where when we started OpenAI, it was not clear how we get to AGI. And we were like, maybe we'll need a bunch of RL agents battling it out on a desert island and consciousness will somehow emerge. But since then, since language modeling has started working, I think the path has become pretty clear. (00:36:48): I guess now the way I think about the challenges are pretty different from how they're laid out in superintelligence. Superintelligence is a lot about how do we keep God in a box and not let the God out. And with language models, it's been kind of both hilarious and terrifying at the same time to see people pulling the God out of the box and being like, "Yeah, come use the whole internet. Here's my bank account, do all sorts of crazy stuff." Just such a different tone from superintelligence. And to be clear, I don't think it's actually that dangerous right now. Our responsible scaling policy defines these AI safety levels that tries to figure out for each level of model intelligence, what is the risk to society. And currently we think we're at ASL-3, which is maybe a little bit risk of harm but not significant. (00:37:44): ASL-4 starts to get to significant loss of human life if a bad actor misuse the technology. And then ASL-5 is potentially extinction level if it's misused or if it is misaligned and does its own thing. We've testified to Congress about how models can do biological uplift in terms of making new pandemics using the models, and that's the A/B test against Google Search. That's like the previous state of the art on uplift trials. And we found that with ASL-3 models, it is actually somewhat significant. It does really help if you wanted to create a bioweapon, and we've hired some experts who actually how to evaluate for those things, but compared to the future, it's not really anything. And I think that's another part of our mission of creating that awareness of saying, "If it is possible to do these bad things, then legislators should know what the risks are." And I think that's part of why we're so trusted in Washington because we've been sort of upfront and clear-eyed about what's going on, what's probably going to happen.
turns.zh:
对我而言，我从小就读了很多科幻小说，这让我养成了从长远角度思考问题的习惯。许多科幻书籍都描绘了人类成为多星系文明、拥有极其先进技术、在太阳周围建造戴森球并用有感知能力的机器人协助人类的场景。正因如此，从那个虚构世界走出来，我并不觉得想象机器能思考是件难事。然而，2016年左右读到尼克·博斯特罗姆的《超级智能》一书时，这一设想才真正变得触手可及。他详细描述了用当时我们所掌握的优化技术训练的人工智能系统，要想实现与人类价值观的共鸣是多么艰难的一件事。从那以后，我对这个问题的评估实际上大幅下调了，因为语言模型如今确实能从根本上理解人类价值观。  

（00:35:55）：这个问题肯定尚未解决，但我比以前更有希望了。但自从读了那本书后，我立刻决定加入OpenAI。当时那只是一家名不见经传的小型研究实验室。我之所以知道它，只因为我的朋友认识当时的CTO格雷格·布罗克曼。埃隆当时在场，而山姆却并不常在。那个组织与现在大不相同。不过随着时间推移，我认为安全问题已经变得更加具体化。当我们创立OpenAI时，AGI的实现路径尚不明朗。我们曾设想，或许需要让一群强化学习智能体在荒岛上相互竞争，意识或许会自然产生。但自从语言模型取得成功后，路径已然清晰。  

（00:36:48）：我想现在我对挑战的看法与《超级智能》中的描述大不相同。《超级智能》主要讲的是如何把“上帝关在笼子里”，不让它跑出来。而语言模型的情况则既令人捧腹又令人恐惧——人们把“上帝”从笼子里放出来，然后说：“好吧，用整个互联网吧。这是我的银行账户，随便做些疯狂的事。”这与《超级智能》完全是两种语气。说实话，我认为当下其实没那么危险。我们的负责任扩展政策定义了人工智能安全等级，试图为每个模型智能级别量化对社会的风险。目前我们认为处于ASL-3级别，风险尚可控制，但不算严重。ASL-4级别若被恶意利用，将导致重大生命损失。ASL-5级别则可能引发灭绝级灾难。我们已向国会作证，说明模型如何通过生物进化实验制造新疫情，这相当于对Google搜索的A/B测试。这是当前生物进化实验的先进水平。我们发现ASL-3级别模型确实存在一定风险，确实能助力制造生物武器。我们聘请了专业评估人员，但与未来相比，这根本不算什么。我认为这也是我们使命的一部分——让人们意识到：“如果做坏事成为可能，立法者就应该了解其中的风险。”我想这也是我们在华盛顿深受信任的原因之一，因为我们始终保持坦诚和清醒的态度。
关于当前局势，以及接下来可能发生的情况。
