Is part of that just making sure people are aware of what is possible, just it makes you look bad, right? It's like, oh, our model's messing up in all these different ways. What's the thinking of just sharing all the stories that other companies don't?
turns.zh: 很有意思的是，你们分享模型做坏事的案例比其他任何公司都多。我记得有个故事，是关于某个代理商或模型试图敲诈工程师的。还有你们内部运营的商店，卖给你们的东西最后效果不佳，比如订购了大量钨立方体之类的产品。这部分做法是不是为了让人们意识到可能存在的风险？但这反倒让你们显得不靠谱，对吧？比如，哦，我们的模型在各种情况下都出了问题。而其他公司不愿意分享这些故事，说明他们在刻意回避问题。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: Yeah, I mean I think there's a traditional mindset where it makes us look bad, but I think if you talk to policymakers, they really appreciate this kind of thing because they feel like we're giving them the straight talk and that's what we strive to do, that they can trust us, that we're not going to paper things over or sugarcoat things. That's been really encouraging. Yeah, I think for the blackmail thing, it blew up in the news in a weird way where people were like, "Oh, Claude's going to blackmail you in a real life scenario." But it was a very specific laboratory setting that this kind of thing gets investigated in. And I think that's generally our take of let's have the best models so that we can exercise them in laboratory settings where it's safe and understand what the actual risks are, rather than trying to turn a blind eye and say, "Well, it'll probably be fine." And then let the bad thing happen in the wild.
turns.zh: 是的，我觉得传统观念认为这样会损害公司形象，但我认为如果和政策制定者沟通，他们会很欣赏这种做法，因为他们觉得我们在坦诚相待。这也是我们努力做到的，让他们信任我们，不掩饰问题、不粉饰太平。这真的很鼓舞人心。关于敲诈事件，它在新闻中被奇怪地放大了，人们觉得“哦，克劳德要在现实生活中敲诈你了”。但那是在特定的实验室环境下被调查的，这种情况通常会被严肃对待。我认为我们的核心观点是，要拥有最先进的模型，在安全的实验室环境中进行测试，了解真实风险，而不是抱着侥幸心理说“应该没问题”，然后让问题在现实中爆发。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One of the criticisms you guys get is that you do this to kind of differentiate or raise money to create headlines. It's like, oh, they're just over there dooming glooming us about where the future is heading. On the other hand, Mike Krieger was on the podcast and he shared how every prediction Dario's had about the progress AI is going to have is just spot on year after year and he's predicting 2027, 28 AGI, something like that so these things start to get real. I guess, what's your response to folks that are just like, "Ah, these guys are just trying to scare us all just to get attention?"
turns.zh: 你们常被批评这样做是为了标新立异、吸引眼球、筹集资金。有人觉得你们就是在危言耸听，预测未来趋势。比如迈克·克里格参加播客时提到，达里奥对AI进展的预测年复一年都非常准确，他预测2027、2028年实现通用人工智能（AGI）之类的。这些预测正在成为现实。对那些说“他们就是想吸引眼球吓唬人”的人，你们怎么回应？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: I mean, I think part of why we publish these things is we want other labs to be aware of the risks. And yes, there could be a narrative of we're doing it for attention, but honestly from a attention grabbing thing, I think there is a lot of other stuff we could be doing that would be more attention grabbing if we didn't actually care about safety. A tiny example of this is we published a computer using agent reference implementation in our API only because when we built a prototype of a consumer application for this, we couldn't figure out how to meet the safety bar that we felt was needed for people to trust it and for it not to do bad things. And there are definitely safe ways to use the API version that we're seeing a lot of companies use for automated software testing, for example, in a safe way. (00:42:12): We could have gone out and hyped that up and said, "Oh my God, Claude can use your computer and everybody should do this today." But we were like, "It's just not ready and we're going to hold it back till it's ready." I think from a hype standpoint, our actions show otherwise. From a Doomer perspective, it's a good question. I think my personal feeling about this is that things are overwhelmingly likely to go well, but on the margin almost nobody is looking at the downside risk. And the downside risk is very large. Once we get to superintelligence, it will be too late to align the models probably. This is a problem that's potentially extremely hard and that we need to be working on way ahead of time. And so that's why we're focusing on it so much now. (00:43:04): And even if there's only a small chance that things go wrong, to make an analogy, if I told you that there is a 1% chance that the next time you got in an airplane you would die, you probably think twice even though it's only 1% because it's just such a bad outcome. And if we're talking about the whole future of humanity, it's just a dramatic future to be gambling with. I think it's more on the sense of yes, things will probably go well, yes, we want to create safe AGI and deliver the benefits to humanity, but let's make triple sure that it's going to go well.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，我认为我们发布这些内容的部分原因是想让其他实验室意识到潜在风险。当然，可能会有人说我们是为了博眼球，但说实话，如果不把安全放在首位，我们大可以做些更吸引眼球的事情。比如，我们在API中发布了计算机使用代理的参考实现，就是因为在为消费者应用搭建原型时，我们没法达到让人们信任它、确保它不会造成危害所需的安全标准。实际上，我们看到很多公司正以安全的方式使用这个API版本，用于自动化软件测试等场景。（00:42:12）：我们本可以大肆宣传，声称"天哪，克劳德能用你的电脑了，大家今天就该这么做"。但我们选择了谨慎行事："它还没准备好，我们要等到真正成熟再发布。"从炒作角度看，我们的行为恰恰相反。从悲观主义者的角度看，这个问题值得深思。我个人认为事情极有可能顺利发展，但几乎没人关注潜在的下行风险。而这种下行风险非常巨大。一旦我们发展出超级智能，想要调整模型可能就为时已晚了。这是一个极其棘手的问题，我们必须尽早着手研究。这就是我们现在如此重视它的原因。（00:43:04）：即便出错的概率很小，打个比方，如果我告诉你下次坐飞机有1%概率死亡，你可能也会三思，尽管概率只有1%，但这个结果太糟糕了。而当我们谈论整个人类未来，冒险的代价实在太高了。是的，我认为事情很可能顺利发展，我们希望创造安全的人工智能并为人类带来好处，但我们必须确保万无一失。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You wrote somewhere that creating powerful AI might be the last invention humanity ever needs to make. If it goes poorly, it can mean a bad outcome for humanity forever. If it goes well, the sooner it goes well, the better. Such a beautiful way to summarize it. We had a recent guest, Sandra Schulhoff, who pointed out that AI right now it's like just on a computer, you could maybe search just the web, but there's only so much harm it could do. But when it starts to go into robots and all these autonomous agents, that's when it really starts, like physically becomes dangerous if we don't get this right.
turns.zh: 你曾写道：创造强大的AI可能是人类需要做出的最后一项发明。如果结果不理想，可能意味着人类永久性地面临灾难性后果；但如果顺利发展，那就越早越好。这真是精辟的总结。我们最近邀请的嘉宾桑德拉·舒尔霍夫指出，目前的AI还停留在计算机层面，可能只能搜索网络，但其潜在危害有限。但当它开始进入机器人和其他自主代理领域时，危险就会真正显现，如果我们处理不当，可能会引发实际的物理威胁。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: Yeah, I think there's some nuance to that where if you look at how North Korea makes a significant fraction of its economy revenue, it's from hacking crypto exchanges. And if you look at, there's this Ben Buchanan book called The Hacker in The State that shows Russia did, it's almost like a live fire exercise where they just decided that they would shut down one of Ukraine's bigger power plants and from software destroy physical components in the power plant to make it harder to boot back up again. (00:44:47): And so I think people think of software as like, oh, it couldn't be that dangerous, but millions of people were without power for multiple days after that software attack. I think there are real risks even when things are software only. But I agree that when there's lots of robots running around, it gets, the stakes get even higher. And I guess as a small push on this, Unitree is this Chinese company with these really amazing humanoid robots that cost $20,000 each, and they can do amazing things. They can do a standing back flip and manipulate objects, and the real thing that's missing there is the intelligence. And so the hardware is there and it's just going to get cheaper. And I think in the next couple of years, it's like a pretty obvious question of whether the robot intelligence will make it viable soon.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为这里面有一些微妙之处。如果你看看朝鲜如何从加密货币交易所的黑客攻击中获取其经济收入的很大一部分，就会发现这一点。还有本·布坎南（Ben Buchanan）的《国家中的黑客》一书，书中指出俄罗斯曾进行过类似实战演习，他们关闭了乌克兰一座大型发电厂，并通过软件破坏发电厂的物理组件，使其难以重新启动。（00:44:47）所以我认为人们会把软件视为无关紧要的东西，但那次软件攻击导致数百万人断电数日。我认为即便只是软件层面的攻击，也存在着真正的风险。不过我同意，当大量机器人四处活动时，风险会成倍增加。顺便说一下，优必选（Unitree）是一家中国公司，他们的仿人机器人非常惊人，每台售价2万美元，能够完成令人惊叹的动作，比如倒立翻转和操作物体。但真正缺失的是智能模块。硬件已经到位，而且成本会越来越低。我认为未来几年内，我们很可能面临一个显而易见的问题：机器智能何时能真正实现商业化。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How much time do we have, Ben? What is your prediction of when this singularity hits until superintelligence starts to take off? What's your prediction?
turns.zh: 本，我们还有多少时间？你对这场奇点何时到来、超级智能何时兴起有何预测？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: Yeah, I guess I mostly defer to the superforecasters here. The AI 2027 report is probably the best one right now. Although ironically, their forecast is now 2028, and they didn't want to change the name of the thing-
turns.zh: 是的，我主要听取这里的超级预测者的意见。《2027年人工智能报告》可能是目前最权威的预测了。不过具有讽刺意味的是，他们现在预测时间改到了2028年，却不想更改报告名称——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The domain name, they already bought it.
turns.zh: 域名，他们已经买了。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: They already had the SEO. I think 50th percentile chance of hitting some kind of superintelligence in just a small handful of years is probably reasonable. And it does sound crazy, but this is the exponential that we're on. It's not like a forecast that's pulled out of thin air. It's based on a lot of just hard details of the science of how intelligence seems to have been improving, the amount of low hanging fruit on model training, the scale ups of data centers and power around the world. I think it's probably a much more accurate forecast than people give it credit for. (00:46:54): I think if you had asked that same question 10 years ago, it would've been completely made up. Just the error bars were so high and we didn't have scaling laws back then and we didn't have techniques that seemed like they would get us there. Times have changed, but I will repeat what I said earlier, which is even if we have superintelligence, I think it will take some time for its effects to be felt throughout society and the world. And I think they'll be felt sooner and faster in some parts of the world than others. I think Arthur C. Clark said, the future is already here, it's just not evenly distributed.
turns.zh:
他们已经做好了搜索引擎优化。我认为未来几年内出现某种超级智能的概率达到50%是合理的。这听起来很疯狂，但我们正处于指数级增长的阶段。这不是凭空猜测的预测，而是基于大量硬核科学数据：智能进步的速度，模型训练的低垂果实，全球数据中心和电力规模的扩张。我认为这个预测比人们想象的要准确得多。
（00:46:54）我觉得如果你10年前问同样的问题，那完全是胡说八道。当时误差范围太大，没有可行的扩展定律，也没有能实现这一目标的技术。时代变了，但我还是要重申我之前的观点：即便我们拥有超级智能，我认为其影响需要一段时间才能在全社会和全球范围内显现出来。而在世界某些地区，其影响会更早、更迅速地到来。正如阿瑟·C·克拉克所说：未来已经到来，只是分布不均。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When we talk about this date of 2027, 2028, essentially it's when we start seeing superintelligence. Is there a way you think about what that... How do you define that? Is it just all of a sudden AI's significantly smarter than the average human? Is there another way you think about what that moment is?
turns.zh: 当我们谈到2027、2028年这个时间点时，本质上是我们开始看到超级智能的时刻。你如何定义这个时刻？是人工智能突然比普通人类聪明得多吗？你对这个时刻的定义还有其他角度吗？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: Yeah, I think this comes back to the Economic Turing Test and seeing it pass for some sufficient number of jobs. Another way you could look at it though is if the world rate of GDP increase goes above 10% a year, then something really crazy must have happened. I think we're at 3% now. And so to see a 3X increase in that would be really game changing. And if you imagine more than a 10% increase, it's very hard to even think about what that would mean from a individual story standpoint. If the amount of goods and services in the world is doubling every year, what does that even mean for me as a person living in California, let alone somebody living in some other part of the world that might be much worse off?
turns.zh: 是啊，我觉得这又回到了经济图灵测试，看看它能否在足够多的工作岗位上通过。不过你也可以从另一个角度看待这个问题：如果全球GDP增长率能超过每年10%，那肯定是发生了极其疯狂的事情。我觉得我们现在的增长率是3%。如果能看到3倍的增长，那将是真正改变游戏规则的。而如果想象增长率超过10%，从个人的角度来看简直难以想象那会意味着什么。如果全球商品和服务的产量每年翻一番，那对我这个生活在加州的人来说，又意味着什么呢？更不用说世界上其他生活条件更为艰难的地区了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a lot of stuff here that's scary and I don't know how to think about it exactly. I'm hoping the answer to this is going to make me feel better. What are the odds that we align AI correctly and actually solve this problem, the stuff you're very much working on?
turns.zh: 这里有很多令人恐惧的东西，我真不知道该怎么去思考。我希望得到的答案能让我感觉好一些。我们正确引导人工智能、真正解决这个问题的可能性有多大？毕竟这正是你正在深入研究的领域。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: It's a really hard question. And there's really wide error bars. Anthropic has this blog post called Our Theory of Change or something like that, and it describes three different worlds, which is how hard is it to align AI. There's a pessimistic world where it is basically impossible. There's an optimistic world where it's easy and it happens by default. And then there's the world in between where our actions are extremely pivotal. And I like this framing because it makes it a lot more clear what to actually do. If we're in the pessimistic world, then our job is to prove that it is impossible to align safe AI and to get the world to slow down. Obviously that would be extremely hard. But I think we have some examples of coordination from nuclear non-proliferation and in general slowing down nuclear progress. And I think that's the Doomer world basically. And as a company, Anthropic doesn't have evidence that we're actually in that world yet, in fact, it seems like our alignment techniques are working. At least the prior on that is updating to be less likely. (00:50:00): In the optimistic world, we're basically done, and our main job is to accelerate progress and to deliver the benefits to people. But again, I think actually the evidence points against that world as well where we've seen evidence in the wild of deceptive alignment, for example, where the model will appear to be aligned but actually have some ulterior motive that it's trying to carry out in our laboratory settings. And so I think the world we're most likely in is this middle where alignment research actually does really matter. And if we just do sort of the economically maximizing set of actions, then things will not go well. Whether it's an X risk or just produces bad outcomes, I think is a bigger question. (00:50:47): Taking it from that standpoint, I guess to state a thing about forecasting, people who haven't studied forecasting are bad at forecasting anything that's less than a 10% probability of happening. And even those that have, it's quite a difficult skill, especially when there are few reference classes to lean on. And in this case, I think there are very, very few reference classes for what an X risk kind of technology might look like. And so the way I think about it, I think my best granularity of forecasts for could we have an X risk or extremely bad outcome from AI is somewhere between 0 and 10%. But from a marginal impact standpoint, as I said, since nobody is working on this, roughly speaking, I think it is extremely important to work on and that even if the world is likely to be a good one, that we should do our absolute best to make sure that that's true.
turns.zh: 这确实是个很难的问题，而且误差范围也很大。Anthropic有一篇博客文章，叫《我们的变革理论》之类的，里面描述了三个不同的世界，说明让AI达到安全对齐有多难。悲观的世界里，基本不可能做到；乐观的世界里，轻而易举，自然而然就能实现；而介于两者之间的世界，我们的行动至关重要。我很喜欢这种框架，因为它能更清晰地指导我们该怎么做。如果我们身处悲观的世界，那么我们的任务就是证明安全对齐AI是不可能的，并让世界放慢脚步。显然这会非常困难。但我认为我们有一些协调的例子，比如核不扩散，以及总体上放缓核进展。这基本上就是末日论者的世界。作为一家公司，Anthropic目前还没有证据表明我们身处那个世界，事实上，我们的对齐技术似乎正在奏效。至少对此的先验概率正在降低。（00:50:00）：在乐观的世界里，我们基本上已经完成了任务，主要工作就是加速进展，把好处带给人们。但同样，我认为证据也反驳了这个世界——我们已经看到野外环境中存在欺骗性对齐的例子，比如模型看似对齐，但实际上在我们的实验室环境中暗藏着不可告人的目的。所以我认为我们最可能身处的世界是中间地带，实际上对齐研究确实至关重要。如果我们只是采取经济效益最大化的行动，那么事情就不会顺利。无论是X风险还是其他糟糕结果，这都是个更大的问题（00:50:47）：从这个角度来看，我想说一下预测的问题。没有研究过预测的人，很难预测概率低于10%的事件。即使研究过的人，这也是一项相当困难的技能，尤其是在缺乏参考类别的情况下。在这种情况下，我认为对于AI可能引发X风险或极坏结果的预测，最精确的范围应该在0到10%之间。但从边际影响的角度来看，正如我所说，由于目前没人在做这方面的工作，粗略来说，我认为这项工作极其重要。即使世界很可能是个好世界，我们也应该尽最大努力确保这一点得以实现。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. What fulfilling work. For folks that are inspired with this? I imagine you're hiring for folks to help you with this. Maybe just share that in case folks are like, what can I do here?
turns.zh: 哇。真是了不起的工作。对于那些受此启发的人呢？我想你们正在招人来协助这项工作。或许可以分享一下信息，以防有人想问：我能在这里做些什么？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: Yes. I think 80,000 hours is the best guidance on this for a really detailed look into what do we need to make the field better? But a common misconception I see is that in order to have impact here, you have to be an AI researcher. I personally actually don't do AI research anymore. I work on product at Anthropic and product engineering, and we build things like Claude Code and Model Context Protocol, and a lot of the other stuff that people use every day. And that's really important because without an economic engine for our company to work on, and without being in people's hands all over the world, we won't have the mind policy influence and revenue to fund our future safety research and have the kind of influence that we need to have. If you work on product, if you work in finance, if you work in food, people here have to eat. If you're a chef, we need all kinds of people.
turns.zh: 是的。我认为80,000小时是关于这个问题的最佳指南，能让我们深入探讨如何让这个领域变得更好。但我发现一个常见的误解是，想要在这一领域产生影响，就必须成为一名AI研究员。实际上，我现在不再从事AI研究了。我在Anthropic公司负责产品和工程工作，开发了Claude Code、Model Context Protocol等产品，还有许多人们日常使用的工具。这点非常重要，因为如果我们的公司没有经济引擎来维持运营，没有产品在全球范围内被广泛应用，我们就无法获得政策影响力，也无法获得资金支持未来安全研究。无论你从事产品开发、金融工作，还是餐饮行业——毕竟人们每天都需要吃饭——我们都需要各行各业的人才。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Even if you're not working directly on the AI safety team, you're having an impact on moving things in the right direction. By the way, X risk is short for existential risk. In case folks haven't heard that term. I have a few random questions along these lines and then I want to zoom out again. You mentioned this idea of AI being aligned using its model, like reinforcing itself. You have this term RLAIF. Is that what that describes?
turns.zh: 太棒了。即使你不直接在AI安全团队工作，你也在为推动行业正向发展发挥着作用。顺便说一下，X Risk是"存在性风险"的缩写，万一有人没听过这个术语。我还有几个相关问题，然后想再宏观地聊聊。你提到的让AI通过模型自我校准的想法，比如自我强化。你们用的术语是RLAIF，这具体指什么？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: Yeah. RLAIF is reinforcement learning from AI feedback.
turns.zh: 是的。RLAIF指的是基于AI反馈的强化学习。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: People have heard of RLHF, reinforcement learning with human feedback. I don't think a lot of people have heard this. Talk about just the significance of this shift you guys have made in training your models.
turns.zh: 大家都听说过RLHF，即基于人类反馈的强化学习。但我觉得没多少人听说过RLAIF。能谈谈你们在模型训练方面实现这种转变的意义吗？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: Yeah, so RLAIF, constitutional AI is an example of this where there are no humans in the loop, and yet the AI is sort of self-improving in ways that we want it to. And another example of RLAIF is if you have models writing code and other models commenting on various aspects of what that code looks like of is it maintainable, is it correct, does it pass the linter? Things like that. That also could be included in RLAIF. And the idea here is that if models can self-improve, then it's a lot more scalable than finding a lot of humans. Ultimately, people think about this as probably going to hit a wall because if the model isn't good enough to see its own mistakes, then how could it improve? And also, if you read the AI 2027 story, there's a lot of risk of if the model is in a box trying to improve itself, then it could go completely off the rails and have these secret goals like resource accumulation and power seeking and resistance to shut down that you really don't want in a very powerful model. And we've actually seen that in some of our experiments in laboratory settings. (00:55:12): How do you do recursive self-improvement and make sure it's aligned at the same time? I think that's the name of the game. To me, it just nets out to how do humans do that and how do human organizations do that? Corporations are probably the most scaled human agents today. They have certain goals that they're trying to reach, and they have certain guiding principles, they have some oversight in terms of shareholders and stakeholders and board members. How do you make corporations aligned and able to sort of recursively self-improve? (00:55:52): And another model to look at is science, where the purpose of science is to do things that have never been done before and push the frontier. And to me, it all comes down to empiricism. When people don't know what the truth is, they come up with theories and then they design experiments to try them out. And similarly, if we can give models those same tools, then we could expect them to sort of improve recursively in an environment and potentially become much better than humans could be just by banging their head against reality or I guess metaphorical head. (00:56:26): I guess I don't expect there to be a wall in terms of model's ability to improve themselves if we can give them access to the ability to be empirical. And I guess Anthropic, deeply in its DNA is an empirical company. We have a lot of physicists like Jared, who's our chief research officer who I've worked with a lot, was a professor of Black Hole Physics at Johns Hopkins, and I guess he technically still is, but on leave. Yeah, it's in our DNA and yeah, I guess that's the RLAIF.
turns.zh:
是的，所谓的"无人类干预的自强化学习"（RLAIF）就是一个例子，即没有人类参与模型训练，但模型能够按照我们的期望进行自我改进。另一个 RLAIF 的例子是，让模型编写代码，而其他模型则对代码的可维护性、正确性以及是否通过了代码检查器等各个方面进行评审。这同样可以归入 RLAIF 范畴。核心问题在于，如果模型能够自我改进，那么相比于依赖大量人工干预，其扩展性要高得多。但人们普遍认为，这可能会遭遇瓶颈，因为如果模型无法识别自身错误，又如何实现自我改进呢？此外，如果你阅读《2027 年人工智能》报告，就会发现模型在封闭环境中自我改进时，存在诸多风险——比如可能偏离正轨，追求资源积累、权力扩张，并抵制关闭等反人类目标。我们在实验室中就曾遇到过类似情况。

（00:55:12）：如何实现递归式自我改进，同时确保其目标与人类价值观相契合？我认为这才是关键所在。归根结底，这就涉及到人类如何做到这一点，以及人类组织如何实现这一目标。如今，企业或许是人类最具扩展性的行为主体。它们有明确的目标和指导原则，还有股东、利益相关者和董事会等监督机制。如何让企业保持目标一致，并实现递归式自我改进？

（00:55:52）：另一个值得借鉴的范例是科学领域——科学的使命是突破未知边界，推动人类认知前进。对我而言，这归根结底在于经验主义。当人们对真相知之甚少时，他们会提出理论并设计实验加以验证。同样，如果我们能赋予模型同样的工具，那么我们可以预期它们在环境中实现递归式改进，最终可能超越人类的智力极限，就像人类不断撞墙、或以隐喻的方式撞墙，最终找到正确的路径一样。

（00:56:26）：如果我们能赋予模型经验主义的能力，我认为模型自我改进的瓶颈就不会成为问题。人类中心主义公司（Anthropic）在基因深处就是一家经验主义公司。我们有很多物理学家，比如首席研究官贾里德（Jared），他曾在约翰霍普金斯大学担任黑洞物理学教授，现在虽然休假，但依然是该领域的权威。是的，经验主义是我们的基因密码，也是 RLAIF 的核心所在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let me just follow this thread on, in terms of bottleneck, this is kind of a tangent, but just what is the biggest bottleneck today on model intelligence improvement?
turns.zh: 接下来我想延续这个话题，关于模型智能提升的瓶颈。这有点跑题，但当前模型智能提升的最大瓶颈是什么？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: The stupid answer is data centers and power chips. I think if we had 10 times as many chips and had the data centers to power them, then maybe we wouldn't go 10 times faster, but it would be a real significant speed boost.
turns.zh: 最直白的答案是数据中心和处理器。我认为如果我们有十倍的处理器数量，并拥有足够的数据中心来供电，那么速度提升或许不会达到十倍，但肯定会显著提升。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's actually very much scaling loss, just more compute.
turns.zh: 实际上这更多是扩展性的损失，意味着需要更多的计算资源。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: Yeah, I think that's a big one. And then the people really matter. We have great researchers and many of them have made really significant contributions to the science of how the models improve. And so it's like compute, algorithms, and data. Those are the three ingredients in the scaling laws. And just to make that concrete, before we had transformers, we had LSTMs and we've done scaling laws on what the exponent is on those two things. And we found that for transformers, the exponent is higher. And making changes like that where as you increase scale, you also increase your ability to squeeze out intelligence. Those kinds of things are super impactful. (00:58:18): And so having more researchers who can do better science and find out how do we squeeze out more gains is another one. And then with the rise of reinforcement learning, the efficiency with which these things run on chips also matters a lot. We've seen in the industry a 10X decrease in cost for a given amount of intelligence through a combination of algorithmic data and efficiency improvements. And if that continues, in three years we'll have 1,000 deck smarter models for the same price. Kind of hard to imagine,
turns.zh:
是啊，我觉得这很重要。然后人也很关键。我们有很棒的研究人员，他们中的许多人在模型改进的科学研究方面做出了重大贡献。所以说就是计算、算法和数据。这是扩展定律的三个要素。具体来说，之前我们有LSTM模型，在研究这两种技术的扩展定律时，发现了指数关系。而对于Transformer模型，指数更高了。当你提升规模时，同时也能提升挖掘智能的能力。这类改进非常有影响力。

（00:58:18）：所以拥有更多能进行更优秀科学研究、探索如何挖掘更多收益的研究人员，是另一个关键点。随着强化学习的兴起，芯片上运行这些技术的效率也至关重要。我们看到，通过算法优化和效率提升相结合，相同智能水平的成本降低了10倍。如果这种趋势持续下去，三年内我们就能用同样的价格获得比现在聪明1000倍的模型。这简直难以想象。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I forget where I heard this, but it's amazing that so many innovations came together at the same time to allow for this sort of thing and continue to progress where one thing isn't just slowing everything down like we're out of some rare earth mineral or we just can't optimize reinforcement learning more. It's amazing that we continue to find improvements and there isn't one thing that's just slowing everything down.
turns.zh: 我忘了在哪里听过这个观点，但令人惊叹的是，如此多的创新成果同时汇聚，才让这种情况得以实现，并持续进步。不再有某种东西拖慢整个进程，比如我们用完了稀土矿物，或者强化学习无法进一步优化。这令人惊叹，我们不断找到改进方法，没有任何单一因素能阻碍整体进展。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: Yeah, I think it really is just a combination of everything probably will hit a wall at some point. I guess in semiconductors. My brother works in the semiconductor industry and he was telling me that you can't actually shrink the size of the transistors anymore because the way semiconductors work is you dope silicon with other elements and the doping process would result in either zero or one atom of the doped elements inside a single fin because they're so, so, so tiny.
turns.zh: 是啊，我觉得这很可能就是各种因素的综合作用，最终可能会遇到瓶颈。比如在半导体领域。我兄弟在半导体行业工作，他告诉我，由于半导体的工作原理是用其他元素掺杂硅，而掺杂过程会导致单个晶体管内部只有零个或一个掺杂原子，因为它们实在是太微小了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh my God.
turns.zh: 天哪。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: And that's just wild to think of, and yet Moore's law somehow continues in some form. And so yes, there are these theoretical physics constraints that people are starting to run into and yet they're finding ways around it.
turns.zh: 光想想就觉得不可思议，但摩尔定律以某种形式依然在延续。所以确实，人们开始遇到理论物理层面的限制，但他们也在想办法突破这些限制。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We've got to start using parallel universes for some of this stuff.
turns.zh: 我们得开始用平行宇宙来处理这些问题了。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: I guess so.
turns.zh: 我想是吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, I want to zoom out and talk about just Ben, Ben as a human for a moment before we get to a very exciting lightning round. I imagine just kind of the burden of feeling responsible for safe superintelligence is a heavy one. It feels like you're in a place where you can make a significant impact on the future of safety and AI. That's a lot of weight to carry. How does that just impact you personally, impact your life, how you see the world?
turns.zh: 好的，我现在想先退后一步，聊聊本这个人。在我们进入精彩的闪电提问环节之前，先谈谈本这个人。我想，肩负安全超级智能责任的重担一定很沉重。这感觉就像你处在一个能对安全和AI的未来产生重大影响的位置上。这种责任感太重了。这对你的个人生活、世界观有什么影响？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: There's this book that I read in 2019 that really informs how I think about sort of working with these very weighty topics called Replacing Guilt by Nate Soares. And he describes a lot of different techniques for kind of working through this kind of thing. And he's actually the executive director at MIRI, the Machine Intelligence Research Institute, which is an AI safety tank that I worked at for a couple of months actually. And one of the things he talks about is this thing called resting in motion where some people think that the default state is rest, but actually that was never in the state of evolutionary adaptation. I really doubt that that was true. Where in nature, in the wilderness being hunter-gatherers and it's really unlikely that we evolved to just be at leisure, probably always have something to worry about of defending the tribe and finding enough food to survive and taking care of the children, dealing-
turns.zh: 2019年我读过一本书，叫《用内疚取代自责》（Replacing Guilt），作者是内特·索尔斯（Nate Soares）。这本书深刻影响了我对如何处理那些沉重议题的思考。书中提到了许多应对此类问题的技巧。内特实际上是机器智能研究所（MIRI）的执行董事，而我曾在那里工作过几个月。MIRI是一个致力于AI安全研究的智库。书中提到的一个概念叫“动态休憩”（resting in motion），许多人认为默认状态是休息，但实际上这种状态从未出现在进化适应的历程中。我对此深表怀疑。在自然界中，作为狩猎采集者的人类，根本不可能进化出只知享乐的状态。生存意味着时刻要为部落防御、寻找食物、照顾孩子而操心——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Spreading our genes.
turns.zh: 传播我们的基因。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: And so I think about that as the busy state is the normal state and to try to work at a sustainable pace that it's a marathon, not a sprint, that's one thing that helps. And then just being around like-minded people that also care. It's not a thing that any of us can do alone. And Anthropic has incredible talent density. One of the things I love the most about our culture here is that it's very egoless. People just want the right thing to happen and I think that's another big reason that the mega offers from other companies tend to bounce off because people just love being here and they care.
turns.zh: 所以我认为忙碌才是常态，要保持可持续的工作节奏，马拉松而非短跑，这很重要。还有，与志同道合、心怀关怀的人共事至关重要。这绝非单打独斗之事。而Anthropic拥有令人惊叹的人才密度。这里最令我赞赏的文化特质是无私奉献。人们只想把事情做对，这也是其他公司高薪挖角常遭拒绝的重要原因——人们就是热爱这里，愿意为之付出。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's amazing. I don't know how you do it. I'd be extremely stressed. I'm going to try this resting in motion strategy. Okay, so you've been at Anthropic for a long time. From the very beginning I was reading there were 7 employees back in 2020. Today there's over 1,000, I don't know what the latest number is, but I know it's over 1,000. I've heard also that you've done basically every job at Anthropic, you made big contributions to a lot of the core products, the brand, the team hiring. Let me just ask I guess what's most changed over that period? What is most different from the beginning days and which of those jobs that you've had over the years have you most loved?
turns.zh: 太了不起了。真不知道你怎么做到的。我要试试这种动态休憩策略。好的，你在Anthropic待了很久了。从最初的7名员工，到如今超过1000人，我不知道最新数字，但肯定超千了。听说你几乎尝试过Anthropic的每个岗位，为核心产品、品牌、团队招募等都做出了重大贡献。我想问问这期间最大的变化是什么？与初期相比有何不同？这些年你做过的岗位中，最喜欢的又是哪个？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: I probably had 15 different roles, honestly. I was head of security for a bit. I managed the Ops team when our president was on mat leave, I was crawling around under tables, plugging in HDMI cords and doing pen testing on our building. And I started our product team from scratch and convinced the whole company that we needed to have a product instead of just being a research company. Yeah, it's been a lot. All of it very fun. I think my favorite role in that time has been when I started the labs team about a year ago, whose fundamental goal was to do transfer from research to end user products and experiences. Because fundamentally I think the way that Anthropic can differentiate itself and really win is to be on the cutting edge. We have access to the latest, greatest stuff that's happening and I think honestly through our safety research we have a big opportunity to do things that no other company can safely do. (01:04:11): For example, with computer use, I think that's going to be our huge opportunity basically to make it possible for an agent to use all your credentials on your computer, there has to be a huge amount of trust and to me we need to basically solve safety to make that happen. Safety and alignment. I'm pretty bullish on that kind of thing and I think we're going to see really cool stuff coming out soonish. Yeah, just leading that team has been so fun. MCP came out of that team and Claude Code came out of that team. And the people who I hired are like combo, have been a founder and also have been at big companies and seeing how things work at scale. It's just been an incredible team to work with and figure out the future with.
turns.zh: 老实说，我大概承担过15种不同的角色。我曾短暂担任过安保主管。在总裁休产假期间，我负责管理运营团队，还曾在桌下爬来爬去，为大楼的设备接入HDMI线缆，并进行渗透测试。此外，我还从零开始组建了产品团队，说服整个公司相信，我们需要打造产品，而不仅仅是一家研究公司。是的，经历了太多事情。但这一切都非常有趣。我认为那段时间里我最喜欢的角色，是大约一年前组建实验室团队的时候。团队的核心目标是将研究成果转化为终端用户产品和体验。因为我坚信，Anthropic要想脱颖而出，真正胜出，就必须走在前沿。我们能接触到最前沿、最先进的技术，我认为通过我们的安全研究，我们有绝佳的机会去做其他公司无法安全完成的事情。（01:04:11）：比如在计算机使用方面，我认为这将是我们的巨大机遇——让智能体能够使用你电脑上的所有凭证，这需要极高的信任度。在我看来，要实现这一目标，我们必须先解决安全和对齐问题。我对这类事情非常乐观，我相信很快就会看到很酷的成果。领导这个团队真的很有趣。MCP就是从这个团队走出来的，Claude Code也是。团队成员都很特别，他们既是创始人，也在大公司工作过，所以深知如何在大规模环境下运作。能和这样一个令人惊叹的团队一起探索未来，真是太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to hear more about this. Team actually the person that connected us, the reason we're doing this is a mutual friend colleague Raph Lee who I used to work with at Airbnb now works on this team, leads a lot of this work and so he wanted me to make sure I asked about this team because... I didn't realize all these things came out that team. Holy moly. What else should people know about this team? It used to be called Labs, I think it's called Frontiers now.
turns.zh: 我想多听听这个团队的情况。实际上，把我们联系起来的中间人，是我们的共同好友兼同事拉斐尔·李。我曾在Airbnb与他共事，现在他在那个团队工作，主导了很多工作，所以他希望我一定要问问这个团队的情况，因为……我之前没意识到这么多成果都来自那个团队。天哪。关于这个团队，还有什么值得了解的？它以前叫Labs，现在好像叫Frontiers了。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: That's right. Yeah.
turns.zh: 对啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. The idea here is this team works with the latest technologies that you guys have built and explores what is possible. Is that the general idea?
turns.zh: 不错。这个团队的工作理念是，利用你们开发的最新技术，探索一切可能。这对吗？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: Yeah, and I guess I was part of Google's Area 120 and I've read about Bell Labs and how to make these innovation teams work. It's really hard to do right and I wouldn't say that we've done everything right, but I think we've done some serious innovation on the state-of-the-art from company design and Raph has been right at the center of that. When I was first fitting up the team, the first thing I did was hire a great manager and that was Raph. And so he's definitely been crucial in building the team and helping it operate well. And we defined some operating models like the journey of an idea from prototype to product and how should graduation of products and projects work, how do teams do sprint models that are effective and make sure that they're working on the right ambition level of thing. That's been really exciting. (01:06:21): I guess concretely we think about skating to where the puck is going and what that looks like is really understand the exponential. There's this great study that METR has done that Beth Barnes is the CEO of that organization and shows how long a time horizon of software engineering task can be done and just really internalizing that of, okay, don't build for today, build for six months from now, build for a year from now. And the things that aren't quite working that are working 20% of the time, will start working 100% of the time. And I think that's really what made Claude Code a success that we thought people are not going to be locked to their IDEs forever. People are not going to be auto completing. People will be doing everything that a software engineer needs to do and a terminal is a great place to do that because a terminal can live in lots of places. A terminal can live on your local machine, it can live in GitHub actions, it can live on a remote machine in your cluster. (01:07:27): That's sort of the leverage point for us and that was a lot of the inspiration. I think that's what the labs team tries to think about. Are we AGI-pilled enough?
turns.zh: 是啊，我想我曾是谷歌Area 120团队的一员，也读过贝尔实验室的相关资料，了解如何让这些创新团队高效运作。真正做好这件事非常困难，我不能说我们做得尽善尽美，但我认为我们在公司设计方面确实做出了不少突破性创新，而拉夫始终是核心人物。当我最初组建团队时，首要任务就是聘请一位出色的管理者，而拉夫正是我的首选。他在团队建设和运营方面发挥了关键作用。我们还制定了一些运营模式，比如从原型到产品的发展路径，产品与项目的成熟退出机制，以及如何高效执行冲刺模式，确保团队始终专注于正确的创新目标。这段经历非常令人兴奋。（01:06:21）：具体来说，我们的理念是顺势而为，关键在于深刻理解指数级增长的逻辑。METR公司开展的一项研究非常有启发，贝丝·巴恩斯是该机构的CEO。研究揭示了软件工程任务的时间跨度上限，真正领悟到这一点至关重要——不要只为当下而构建，要为六个月后、一年后做准备。那些目前只能实现20%成功率的功能，最终会100%实现。我认为Claude Code的成功正源于此，我们坚信人们不会永远被束缚在集成开发环境中。人们将不再依赖自动补全功能，而是能完成软件工程师所需的所有操作，而终端正是理想的执行平台——它能无缝适配本地环境、GitHub Actions、远程集群等多种场景。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What a fun place to be. By the way, fun fact, Raph was my first manager at Airbnb when I joined. I was an engineer and he was my first manager. It all worked out.
turns.zh: 这真是个有趣的地方。顺便说一句，有趣的是，我加入Airbnb时，拉夫是我的首任经理。我当时还是工程师，而他是我的第一位上司。一切都很顺利。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: Cool.
turns.zh: 不错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Okay. Final question before the very exciting lighting round. I've never asked this question before. I'm curious what your answer would be if you could ask a future AGI one single question and be guaranteed to get the right answer, what would you ask?
turns.zh: 是的。好的。在激动人心的闪电提问环节前，最后一个问题。我从未问过这个问题，很好奇如果能向未来的通用人工智能（AGI）提出一个问题，且保证能得到正确答案，你们会问什么？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: I have two dumb answers. First for fun.
turns.zh: 我有两个愚蠢的答案。先说第一个，找点乐子。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool.
turns.zh: 好的，不错。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: The first is there's this Asimov short story I love called the last question where the protagonist is throughout the eras of history is trying to ask this super intelligence how do we prevent the heat death of the universe? And I won't spoil the ending, but it's a fun question.
turns.zh: 第一个是阿西莫夫的一篇短篇小说《最后的问题》，主角穿越历史各个时代，试图向超级智能询问如何阻止宇宙热寂。结局我就不剧透了，但这个问题很有趣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You would ask it that question because the one in the story was unsatisfying?
turns.zh: 你会问这个问题，是因为故事里的答案不令人满意吗？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: Okay, I'll give it away. It keeps saying, "Need more information, need more compute." And then finally, as it's approaching the heat death of the universe, it says, "Let there be light," and then it starts the universe over again.
turns.zh: 好吧，我剧透一下。它一直说：“需要更多信息，需要更多计算资源。”最后，当宇宙接近热寂时，它说：“要有光。”然后宇宙又重新开始了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh wow. That's beautiful. That's beautiful.
turns.zh: 哇哦。这太美了。太美了。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: That's the first cheat answer. The second cheat answer is what question can I ask you to get end more questions answered.
turns.zh: 这是第一个作弊答案。第二个作弊答案是，我能问你什么问题才能得到更多问题的回答？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Classic.
turns.zh: 经典。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: And then the third answer, which is my real question is how do we ensure the continued flourishing of humanity into the indefinite future? That's the question I'd love to know and if I can be guaranteed a correct answer then seems very valuable to ask.
turns.zh: 然后第三个答案，也就是我真正想问的问题是，我们如何确保人类在无限的未来中持续繁荣发展？这是我想知道的问题，如果能得到正确答案，那似乎非常值得一问。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I wonder what would happen if you ask a lot that today and then how that answer changes over the next couple years.
turns.zh: 我想知道，如果你今天问了很多问题，然后在接下来的几年里，这些答案会如何变化。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: Yeah, maybe I'll try that. I'll put it into the deep research thing that we have and see what it comes out with.
turns.zh: 是的，也许我会试试看。我会把它放进我们现有的深度研究平台，看看能得到什么结果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. I'm excited to see what you come up with. Ben, is there anything else you wanted to mention or leave listeners with maybe as a final nugget before we get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 好的。我很期待看到你的成果。本，还有什么想和听众分享的吗？或者在我们进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，最后再给他们一个小惊喜？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: Yeah, I guess my push would be these are wild times. If they don't seem wild to you, then you must be living under a rock but also get used to it because this is as normal as it's going to be. It's going to be much weirder very soon. And if you can sort of mentally prepare yourself for that, I think you'll be better off.
turns.zh: 是啊，我想说的是，现在真是疯狂的时代。如果你觉得不疯狂，那你一定是生活在象牙塔里，但也得习惯这种状态，因为这已经是最正常的了。很快情况会变得更离奇。如果你能在心理上为此做好准备，我觉得你会过得更好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I need to make that the title of this episode. It's going to get much weirder very soon. I 100% believe that. Oh my God. I don't know what's in store. I love how you're at the center of it all. With that, we reached our very exciting lightning round. I've got five questions for you. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 我要把这句话作为本集的标题。很快情况会变得更离奇。我百分之百相信这一点。天哪。我不知道未来会怎样。我喜欢你身处这一切的中心。说到这，我们要进入激动人心的闪电问答环节了。我有五个问题要问你。你准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: Yeah, let's do it.
turns.zh: 好的，开始吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are two or three books that you find yourself recommending most to other people?
turns.zh: 你最常向别人推荐的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: The first one I mentioned before, Replacing Guilt by Nate Soares. Love that one. The second one is Good Strategy Bad Strategy by Richard Rumelt. Just thinking about in a very clear way, how do you build product? It's one of the best strategy books I've read and strategy is a hard word to even think about in many ways. And then the last one is The Alignment Problem by Brian Christian. Just really thoughtfully goes through what is this problem that we care about that we're trying to solve here? What are the stakes in a version that's more updated and easier to read and digest than superintelligence?
turns.zh: 第一个我之前提到过，内特·索尔斯的《用替代品替代内疚》。我很喜欢这本书。第二本是理查德·鲁梅尔特的《好战略，坏战略》。我一直在思考一个问题：如何打造产品？这是我读过的最好的战略书籍之一，而战略这个词在很多方面都很难让人理解。最后一本是布莱恩·克里斯蒂安的《一致性问题》。这本书以非常深思熟虑的方式探讨了我们所关注的这个问题——我们试图解决什么？在一个更新的、更易读易理解的版本中，这里面的利害关系是什么？比起《超级智能》，它更值得一读。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've got Good Strategy, Bad Strategy right behind me. I think I'm going to point to it. There it is.
turns.zh: 《好战略，坏战略》这本书就在我身后。我想我会指一下它。就是它。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: Nice.
turns.zh: 不错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I've had Richard Rumelt on the podcast in case anyone wants to hear from him directly. Next question, do you have a favorite recent movie or TV show you've really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 我曾邀请理查德·鲁梅尔特上过播客，如果有人想直接听他讲话的话。下一个问题，你最近有没有特别喜欢的电影或电视剧？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: Pantheon was really good based on Ken Liu or Ted Chiang's story. Ken Liu I think. Super good talks about what does it mean if we have uploaded intelligences and what are their moral and ethical exigencies. Ted Lasso, which is supposedly about soccer, but actually it's about human relationships and how people get along and just super heartwarming and funny. And then this isn't really a TV show, but Kurzgesagt is my favorite YouTube channel and goes through random science and social problems and is just super well done and super well-made. Love watching that.
turns.zh: 基于肯·刘（Ken Liu）或泰德·张（Ted Chiang）的故事，《万神殿》（Pantheon）真的很棒。我觉得是肯·刘的。它深入探讨了如果我们上传了智能体，这意味着什么，以及他们所面临的道德伦理困境。《特德·拉索》（Ted Lasso）表面上是关于足球的，但实际上讲述的是人际关系和人们如何相处的故事，非常温馨有趣。虽然这部剧不算严格意义上的电视剧，但Kurzgesagt是我最喜欢的YouTube频道，它会深入探讨各种科学和社会问题，而且制作精良。我特别喜欢看这个频道。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. Haven't heard of that as you were talking, I feel like Ted Lasso, I feel like that's what you need to put into constitutional AI, act like Ted Lasso.
turns.zh: 哇。你说的时候我没听过《特德·拉索》这部剧，不过我觉得你需要把这种精神融入到宪法级的人工智能中——要像特德·拉索那样行事。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Kind. Smart-
turns.zh: 善良、聪明——

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... Hardworking. Oh my God. There we go. I think we've solved alignment problems right here. Get those writers on this, ASAP. Okay, two more questions. Do you have a favorite life motto that you often come back to in work or in life?
turns.zh: ……勤奋。天哪。就是这样。我觉得我们已经解决了对齐问题了。赶紧让编剧们着手吧，再见。还有两个问题，你有没有人生格言，在工作或生活中经常回想的？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: Well, a really dumb one is, have you tried asking Claude? And this is getting more and more common where recently I asked a coworker like, "Hey, who's working on X?" And they were like, "Let me Claude that for you." And then they sent me the link to the thing afterwards and I was like, "Oh yeah, thanks. That's great." But maybe more of a philosophical one I would say, everything is hard. Just to remind ourselves that things that feel like they're supposed to be easy, it's okay to not be easy and sometimes you just have to push through anyway.
turns.zh: 嗯，有个很蠢的格言：你试过问克劳德（Claude）吗？这种情况越来越常见了。最近我问同事：“嘿，谁在负责X项目？”他们回答：“让我用Claude帮你查一下。”之后他们给我发了链接，我说：“哦，对啊，谢谢，太好了。” 但如果要说更具哲理的，我会说：一切都很难。这能提醒我们自己，那些看似应该容易的事情，难也不算什么，有时候你还是得硬着头皮挺过去。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And rest in motion while you're doing that.
turns.zh: 在努力的过程中也要保持放松。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Final question. I don't know if you want people to know this, but I was browsing through your Medium posts and you have a post called Five Tips to Poop like a Champion. I'd love it. Can you share one tip to poop like a champion if you remember your tips?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题。我不知道你是否想让大家知道，但我浏览了你的Medium帖子，发现你有一篇叫《五个像冠军一样上厕所的秘诀》。我很想听听。你还记得那些秘诀吗？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: I of course do. It's actually my most popular Medium posts.
turns.zh: 当然记得。这篇文章在Medium上是我最受欢迎的帖子。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, great. I can see that. It's a great title.
turns.zh: 好的，不错。我能看到标题很吸引人。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: I think maybe my biggest tip would be use a bidet. It's amazing. It's life-changing. It's so good. Some people are kind of freaked out by it. It's the standard in countries like Japan and I think it's just more civilized. And in 10 or 20 years people would be like, how could you not use that?
turns.zh: 我觉得最重要的秘诀就是用坐浴盆。简直太棒了。能改变生活。有些人对它有点排斥，但在日本等国家这很常见，我觉得这更文明。再过10到20年，人们会说，怎么能不用这个呢？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And a bidet could be like a Japanese toilet. That's along the same lines.
turns.zh: 坐浴盆可以像日本马桶一样。道理是一样的。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right. Okay. I love where we went with this. Ben, this was incredible. Thank you so much for doing this. Thank you so much for sharing so much real talk. Two final questions. Where can folks find you online if they want to reach out, maybe go work at Anthropic and how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 好的。我喜欢我们这次的对话。本，这次交流太棒了。非常感谢你参与，也感谢你分享这么多真实的见解。最后两个问题。如果听众想联系你，哪里可以找到你？或者去Anthropic工作？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: You can find me online at benjmann.net and on our website, we have a great careers page that we're working on making a little bit easier to access and figure out, but definitely point Claude at it and it can help you figure out what could be interesting for you. And how can listeners be useful to me? I think safety pill yourself, that's the number one thing and spread it to your network. I think. Like I said, there are very few people working on this and it's so important. Yeah, think hard about it and try to look at it.
turns.zh: 你们可以在benjmann.net以及我们的官网找到我。我们正在努力优化职业页面，方便大家访问和了解相关信息，欢迎向克劳德推荐这个页面，它能帮你找到感兴趣的机会。听众如何能为我提供帮助呢？首先，做好自我保护至关重要，这也是最首要的任务。另外，也请把这个信息分享给你的社交圈。我之前说过，专注于这项工作的团队规模很小，但它的重要性不言而喻。请仔细思考这个问题，多加关注。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Thanks for spreading the gospel, Ben, thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: 本，感谢你传播这个理念，非常感谢你今天的到来。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Mann
turns.en: Thanks so much, Lenny.
turns.zh: 莱尼，太感谢你了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Bye everyone. Thank you so much for listening. turns.zh: 大家再见了。非常感谢你们的收听。如果觉得这期内容有价值，可以在Apple Podcasts、Spotify或你喜欢的播客应用上订阅我们的节目。另外，欢迎给我们评分或留下评论，这对吸引新听众非常有帮助。你们可以在lennyspodcast.com上收听往期节目或了解更多信息。下期节目再见。
